Results Interpretation¶

The dataset shows:

  • A dominant cluster of typical songs:

    • moderate danceability & energy
    • low speechiness & instrumentalness

  • Several distinct subgroups:

    • instrumental tracks
    • acoustic songs
    • high-speech (rap/spoken)
    • live recordings

  • This structure strongly supports using clustering, because:

    • There are clear behavioral/music-style differences
    • Many features are informative and varied

In [7]:
corr = X.corr()
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
plt.imshow(corr)
plt.colorbar()
plt.xticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns, rotation=90)
plt.yticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap")
plt.show()

Results Interpretation¶

  • Strong positive relationship:
    • Energy ↔ Loudness (high correlation) → louder songs tend to be more energetic.
  • Moderate positive cluster:
    • Danceability, energy, loudness, and valence are positively related → these likely define a “mainstream/high-energy” cluster.
  • Strong negative relationships:
    • Acousticness vs energy/loudness → acoustic songs are typically quieter and less energetic.
  • Instrumentalness patterns:
    • Positively related to acousticness and negatively to valence/energy → instrumental tracks tend to be calmer and less “happy/high-energy.”
  • Weak correlations overall for some features:
    • Speechiness and liveness show weak relationships with most variables → they may form independent niche clusters.
  • Tempo is relatively independent:
    • Weak correlations with most features → contributes unique variation in clustering.

PCA and K-Means Clustering¶

In [9]:
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95, random_state=42)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

print("Number of PCA components:", pca.n_components_)

plt.plot(np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_), marker='o')
plt.axhline(0.95, linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Number of Components")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Explained Variance")
plt.title("PCA Explained Variance")
plt.show()

Number of PCA components: 8

Results Interpretation¶

  • PCA shows that most of the dataset’s variability can be captured with 5–6 components, allowing effective dimensionality reduction with minimal information loss.
In [10]:
inertias = []
k_values = range(2, 11)

for k in k_values:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    km.fit(X_pca)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

plt.figure()
plt.plot(list(k_values), inertias, marker='o')
plt.xlabel("Number of clusters (k)")
plt.ylabel("Inertia (within-cluster SSE)")
plt.title("Elbow Method for K-Means")
plt.show()

Results Interpretation¶

  • The elbow method suggests an optimal number of clusters around k = 5, where additional clusters provide minimal improvement in reducing within-cluster variance.

Chose k=5 as number of cluster do to drop in slop of curve after

Hierarchical Clustering¶

Results Interpretation¶

Hierarchical Clustering¶

Trying Hierarchical clustering as it builds clusters step-by-step instead of forcing all songs into groups at once like K-means. will show if song groups have a nested structure.

In [24]:
# Dendrogram on a sample (kept smaller so it runs faster and stays readable)
dendro_size = min(300, len(X_pca))
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dendro_idx = rng.choice(len(X_pca), size=dendro_size, replace=False)
X_dendro = X_pca[dendro_idx]

linked = linkage(X_dendro, method='ward')

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
dendrogram(linked, truncate_mode='lastp', p=30)
plt.title('Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Sample)')
plt.xlabel('Cluster')
plt.ylabel('Distance')
plt.show()

Results Interpretation¶

  • Hierarchical clustering confirms that the dataset contains both large-scale divisions and smaller subgroups, reinforcing the validity of using multiple clusters (e.g., k = 5) for detailed segmentation.
In [25]:
# Fit hierarchical clustering on the PCA-reduced data
n_clusters = 5
hier_sample_size = min(3000, len(X_pca))   # lower this if your machine still struggles
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

if len(X_pca) > hier_sample_size:
    hier_idx = rng.choice(len(X_pca), size=hier_sample_size, replace=False)
    X_pca_hier = X_pca[hier_idx]
else:
    hier_idx = np.arange(len(X_pca))
    X_pca_hier = X_pca

agg = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=n_clusters, linkage='ward')
agg_clusters = agg.fit_predict(X_pca_hier)

hier_clustered = X.iloc[hier_idx].copy()
hier_clustered['hier_cluster'] = agg_clusters

print("Hierarchical sample shape:", X_pca_hier.shape)
print("Number of hierarchical labels:", len(agg_clusters))
print("Hierarchical silhouette score:", round(silhouette_score(X_pca_hier, agg_clusters), 4))

PyTorch Autoencoder¶

In [28]:
# Prepare data for PyTorch
X_tensor = torch.tensor(X_scaled, dtype=torch.float32)
dataset = TensorDataset(X_tensor)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
print('Using device:', device)

Using device: cpu

Insights¶

Preparing data for efficient trianing in PyTorch

In [29]:
# Define the autoencoder
class Autoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, latent_dim=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(16, 8),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(8, latent_dim)
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 8),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(8, 16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(16, input_dim)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.encoder(x)
        x_hat = self.decoder(z)
        return x_hat

input_dim = X_scaled.shape[1]
autoencoder = Autoencoder(input_dim=input_dim, latent_dim=3).to(device)
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(autoencoder.parameters(), lr=0.001)

Insights¶

  • allows model to learn a compressed (nonlinear) representation of the data that preserves important structure for tasks like clustering
In [30]:
# Train the autoencoder
num_epochs = 50
loss_history = []

autoencoder.train()
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    epoch_loss = 0.0
    for batch in loader:
        xb = batch[0].to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        reconstructed = autoencoder(xb)
        loss = criterion(reconstructed, xb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        epoch_loss += loss.item() * xb.size(0)

    epoch_loss /= len(dataset)
    loss_history.append(epoch_loss)

    if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0:
        print(f'Epoch {epoch+1}/{num_epochs}, Loss: {epoch_loss:.6f}')

Epoch 10/50, Loss: 0.192956

Compare Clustering Models¶

Below is comparing the original K-means approach, hierarchical clustering, and the deep learning approach (autoencoder + K-means). Higher silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz values are better, while lower Davies-Bouldin values are better.

In [38]:
# KMeans on full PCA
kmeans_sil = silhouette_score(X_pca, clusters)
kmeans_ch  = calinski_harabasz_score(X_pca, clusters)
kmeans_db  = davies_bouldin_score(X_pca, clusters)

# Hierarchical on sampled PCA only
hier_sil = silhouette_score(X_pca_hier, agg_clusters)
hier_ch  = calinski_harabasz_score(X_pca_hier, agg_clusters)
hier_db  = davies_bouldin_score(X_pca_hier, agg_clusters)

# Autoencoder + KMeans on full latent features
ae_sil = silhouette_score(latent_features, ae_clusters)
ae_ch  = calinski_harabasz_score(latent_features, ae_clusters)
ae_db  = davies_bouldin_score(latent_features, ae_clusters)

# Compare clustering methods using internal validation metrics
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": [
        "KMeans on PCA",
        "Hierarchical on PCA sample",
        "Autoencoder + KMeans"
    ],
    "Silhouette Score": [kmeans_sil, hier_sil, ae_sil],
    "Calinski-Harabasz Score": [kmeans_ch, hier_ch, ae_ch],
    "Davies-Bouldin Score": [kmeans_db, hier_db, ae_db]
})

comparison.sort_values(by="Silhouette Score", ascending=False)

Results Interpretation¶

  • Best Overall Model → Autoencoder + KMeans

    • Highest Silhouette: 0.290 → best separation
    • Highest CH score: 46,519 → strongest cluster structure
    • Lowest DB score: 1.103 → least overlap This model clearly produces the most distinct, compact, and well-separated clusters

  • Middle Performance → Hierarchical (PCA Sample)

    • Silhouette: 0.205 → moderate separation
    • CH score: ~538 → very low cluster compactness
    • DB score: 1.647 → noticeable overlap Captures some structure but clusters are weak and less defined

  • Weakest Model → KMeans on PCA

    • Lowest Silhouette: 0.169 → poor separation
    • CH score: 24,130 (moderate but misleading without silhouette)
    • Highest DB: 1.707 → most overlap Clusters are least distinct, even after dimensionality reduction

Takeaways¶

  • Autoencoder significantly improves clustering
    • captures nonlinear relationships that PCA cannot
  • Hierarchical clustering underperforms
    • struggles with overlapping music features
  • PCA + KMeans loses important structure
    • linear reduction removes useful information
